title: Why I Use AI Every Day—and Why Schools Should Too
author: Andrew Marcinek
summary: Andrew Marcinek has used AI every day since November 2022 and argues that schools are making a critical error by conflating two separate problems—phones in pockets and AI in lessons—and banning both rather than building genuine AI literacy. The why-how-at-what-cost framework he developed through three years of daily intentional use is exactly what students need to develop, and banning AI defers that development to no one, leaving students to figure it out alone, unguided, and badly. The path forward mirrors what 1:1 device programs should have done: lead with purpose (what is AI for in this building?), write living policy, and make faculty fluent before students log in—giving teachers the same learning journey that built Marcinek's own judgment.
points: Calling for AI-free schools conflates two distinct problems—phones in pockets and tools in lessons—and the conflation is how good policy goes bad.
Banning AI defers the work of preparing students to use technology effectively, handing that work to no one—which means students do it alone, at home, unguided, and badly.
Schools should learn from 1:1 device failures: procurement-first, purpose-later is why those programs produced backlash; AI gives a chance to run the play correctly the first time.
Before any AI license, schools need a written answer to: what is AI for in our building—thinking partner or answer machine, where assistance ends and authorship begins?
Teachers need access, time, and permission to be novices first; they need the same daily-use learning journey that builds real judgment before their students log in.
quotes: I know what the tool collects about me and about the work I feed into it. I know it isn’t always correct, and that on plenty of tasks the most efficient move is to put it down and think without it.
Why, how, and at what cost — that’s the whole ballgame, and it took me three years of daily, intentional use to build that judgment.
We defer the work of preparing students to use technology effectively and appropriately, and we hand that work to nobody — which means students do it alone, at home, unguided, and badly.
The phone in the pocket and the tool in the lesson are not the same problem, and pretending they are is how good policy goes bad.
We got 1:1 wrong by leading with procurement instead of purpose, and we’re paying for it now with audits, backlash, and bans. AI gives us the chance to run the play correctly the first time.

Your school has to be able to say, out loud and in writing, what it believes AI is for — a thinking partner or an answer machine, where assistance ends and authorship begins, what original work means in your building now.
